rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.7 and 3 report a two-season (2009, 2010) randomized block field experiment in a commercial olive orchard in La Rioja, Argentina, with four irrigation levels (100, 66, 33, 0% ETc) applied through drip lines and measurements of soil water, stem water potential, leaf conductance, sap flow and trunk diameter.
rows.notes: The study uses drip irrigation only as the delivery system for the deficit treatments; it does not compare drip with any other method and does not measure soil evaporation or deep percolation. Its own results concern how soil REW, stem water potential, leaf conductance, sap flow and trunk diameter indices respond to post-harvest regulated deficit irrigation (Figs 2-6) and the signal-to-noise of these indicators (Fig. 7, Table 2). Soil evaporation and Kc values for drip are mentioned only in the Introduction citing earlier work (Rousseaux et al., 2009; Figuerola et al., 2013). No own evidence on drip controlling evaporation or percolation.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2 and 3 report the authors' own two-season field experiment with RDI treatments and measured soil and plant indicators (REW, stem water potential, leaf conductance, sap flow, dendrometer-based MXTD, TGR, MDS).
rows.notes: The study evaluates whether soil moisture and plant-based (trunk diameter) indicators could be used to schedule irrigation (Objective 3; Sections 3.5, 4, 5), concluding that automated soil moisture sensors and continuous trunk diameter recording show potential and that further testing is warranted. It does not implement sensor- or controller-driven dynamic scheduling nor measure water savings from such a system; the reported reductions in annual irrigation (7-20%, Table 1) result from fixed RDI percentages, not sensor-based adjustment. This is a precondition (indicator suitability) of the claimed effect, hence upstream.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a primary field experiment on post-harvest regulated deficit irrigation in olive, assessing soil and plant water-stress indicators for irrigation scheduling; it does not test drip versus other methods, soil evaporation/percolation losses, or automated sensor-based scheduling as such.
